summary: Learners find unknown angles in triangles, quadrilaterals and regular polygons using angle-sum properties — but with the triangle's 180° DERIVED (not merely recalled), the quadrilateral/polygon sums BUILT by partitioning into (n−2) triangles, and the crucial fact that the angle sum is INDEPENDENT of the triangle's size made visible rather than asserted. Activities span a hands-on/manipulable derivation of 180° and size-invariance, a partition-to-build-larger-sums task, scorable missing-angle practice (including 'not drawn to scale' and 360°-distractor items), and a two-step regular-polygon calculation (total sum ÷ vertices). The central danger addressed throughout is teaching '180° in a triangle' as an isolated memorised fact.
misconceptions: Thinks a triangle's angles sum to 360° rather than 180° (documented in diagnostic data), so subtracts from the wrong total.

Believes the angle sum (or a missing angle) depends on the triangle's SIZE — expects a bigger/longer triangle to have larger angles; contradicts the constant 180° sum (documented in children and adults).
Assumes a triangle is isosceles or equilateral because it looks that way on a not-to-scale diagram, so wrongly takes two angles as equal.
Knows '180° in a triangle' only as a disconnected fact and cannot extend it to a quadrilateral or polygon (does not partition into triangles).
For a regular polygon, reports the total angle sum as if it were a single interior angle (forgets to divide by the number of vertices).

activities.title: Torn corners make a straight line (deriving 180°)
steps: Cut or tear the three corners off a paper triangle and arrange them side by side so their vertices meet at a single point — observe that together they fill a straight line (180°), with no visible gap or overlap apart from small paper imperfections.

Alternatively derive the same result by using the longest side as the base: fold the top corner down so it touches the base at the foot of the height, then fold the other two corners in to meet it at that point — they again fill a straight line along the base.
Repeat either method with a differently-shaped triangle (e.g. a long thin one and a squat one) and confirm the three corners again fill a straight line.
On a drag-and-drop screen model, drag the three corner-wedges onto a straight line so they snap to fill 180°, with a banner reading the running sum.
activities.insight: The three interior angles of ANY triangle rearrange to lie on a straight line, so they sum to 180° — this is something you can see happen (by tearing or by folding the corners), not a number to recall.

activities.title: Does the sum change when the triangle changes size?
steps: Predict, before testing: 'If I make this triangle much bigger or stretch it long and thin, will the angle sum get bigger?' Write down your prediction.
Make the triangle larger, then longer and thinner, then squat and wide — on a screen model drag a vertex to reshape it; on paper draw each new triangle.

Each time, re-check the angle sum: read the live sum readout on the screen model, or (on paper) tear or fold the corners of each new triangle, or measure its three marked angles, and record the total.
Compare your prediction with what actually happened to the sum.
activities.insight: The angle sum stays 180° no matter how big, small, long or stretched the triangle is — side length does not change the angle sum, even though many people expect bigger triangles to have bigger angles.

activities.title: Build the polygon sums by cutting into triangles
steps: Draw a diagonal inside a quadrilateral to split it into two triangles (in a dented, non-convex quadrilateral, use the diagonal that stays inside); conclude its angle sum is 2 × 180° = 360°.
Partition a convex pentagon (3 triangles) and a convex hexagon (4 triangles) from one vertex, counting the triangles each time.
Record results in an angle-sum table: triangle 180°, quadrilateral 360°, pentagon 540°, hexagon 720°.
State the pattern in words and as a rule: an n-gon splits into (n−2) triangles, so its angle sum is (n−2) × 180°.
activities.insight: Every simple polygon's (one with no crossing sides) angle sum is built from triangles: an n-sided polygon divides into (n−2) triangles, so its interior angles sum to (n−2) × 180° — the whole family connects back to the triangle.

activities.title: Missing-angle practice, including 'not drawn to scale'
steps: Find a triangle's third angle given two angles by subtracting from 180° (e.g. 180 − (70 + 60) = 50°); write the calculation.
Find a quadrilateral's missing angle by subtracting the three known angles from 360°.
Answer an item deliberately drawn roughly isosceles though it is NOT to scale: compute only from the marked angles, not from how the figure looks and not by measuring the drawing with a protractor.
Sanity-check each answer (each triangle angle must be more than 0° and less than 180°; the three sum to exactly 180°).
activities.insight: Missing angles are found by subtracting known angles from the correct total (180° for a triangle, 360° for a quadrilateral), using the MARKED values rather than the picture's appearance or a protractor reading of a not-to-scale drawing.

activities.title: Regular polygons: find the sum, THEN share it out
steps: For a regular hexagon, first find the total interior-angle sum (4 triangles × 180° = 720°).
Then, because all six interior angles of a regular hexagon are equal, divide: 720° ÷ 6 = 120° for one interior angle.
Write the two steps separately and label which number is the TOTAL sum and which is ONE angle.
Repeat for another regular polygon (e.g. regular pentagon: 540° ÷ 5 = 108°).
activities.insight: For a regular polygon there are two distinct steps: find the total angle sum, then divide equally among the (equal) vertices to get one interior angle — the total sum is not itself a single angle.

checkQuestion: Give the child three figures with angles marked (not to scale). (1) A triangle with two angles 70° and 60°, third unknown — draw it looking roughly isosceles though it isn't. (2) A quadrilateral with three angles marked, one unknown. (3) A regular hexagon, asking for one interior angle. Say: 'Work out each missing angle, and tell me how you got it.' Watch the method — which total they use, whether they partition, whether they trust the picture — without prompting the rules.
checkAnswer: (1) third angle = 180 − (70+60) = 50°, using the triangle sum 180°; (2) missing = 360 − (sum of the three), using the quadrilateral sum 360°; (3) one interior angle = 720° ÷ 6 = 120°, having found the hexagon's angle sum (4 triangles × 180°). Computes from the marked/derived sums, not from appearance, and divides the sum for the regular polygon.
